implementation_notes: jwt-scala is the Scala-first realization: JwtClaim carries issuer, subject, audience, expiration, notBefore, issuedAt and jwtId (with the issuedNow and expiresIn helpers nudging time claims into every token), JwtAlgorithm.RS256 selects the RSA path, and Jwt/JwtJson/JwtCirce/JwtJson4s encode takes the private key and returns the compact assertion; the core is dependency-free and only the JSON module (Circe, Play JSON, Json4s, uPickle) is chosen per project. What replaces the classic structure: the JwtClaim value object plus one encode call replaces the builder class, and Scala's contribution is a typed claim case class that maps into JwtClaim so the profile lives in the type system. On the JVM the Nimbus or Auth0 libraries are equally viable, but then the claim set is built through Java APIs from Scala.
code_sketch:
import pdi.jwt.{Jwt, JwtAlgorithm, JwtClaim}
val claim: JwtClaim = JwtClaim("""{"sub":"user-17","aud":"https://api.example"}""")
  .issuedNow
  .expiresIn(300)
val token: String = Jwt.encode(claim, privateKey, JwtAlgorithm.RS256)
pitfalls: The library deliberately imposes nothing: a JwtClaim with no time claims encodes happily, so a wrapper must add exp (and jti) or assertions become eternal.
String keys go through a simple parser that the README warns about (especially ECDSA); pass PrivateKey/PublicKey/SecretKey objects instead.

Pick one JSON module and use it on both sides: a Circe-produced claim set consumed through the Json4s module works only while the serialization stays byte-compatible, and mixed builds make failures look like signature problems.
